questions.question: Which approach best reflects FNP-level obesity care?
choices: Treat obesity as a chronic multifactorial disease and define patient-centered health and function goals
Prescribe medication based only on a single BMI value
Assume lack of weight loss is lack of effort
Avoid discussing medications, sleep, mental health, or social barriers
questions.explanation: Obesity care is individualized and nonstigmatizing. Assessment includes complications, contributors, patient goals, medications, sleep, mental health, access, and safety.

questions.question: Before adding a weight-management medication for a patient with diabetes who uses insulin and a sulfonylurea, what is most important?
choices: Assume hypoglycemia risk will fall automatically
Review the full glucose-lowering regimen, glucose pattern, food intake, and a coordinated monitoring/dose-adjustment plan
Stop all diabetes medications immediately
Avoid asking about monitoring access
questions.explanation: Incretin-based therapy has low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, but risk can rise with insulin or secretagogues. Safe prescribing requires coordination and monitoring.

questions.question: Which statement about GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy is most accurate?
choices: All products, doses, and indications are interchangeable
They can affect appetite, intake, glucose physiology, and gastric emptying, so exact product labeling and titration matter
They never cause gastrointestinal adverse effects
They should be combined with another incretin product to improve response
questions.explanation: These drugs have related but not identical indications, dosing, and warnings. Product-specific prescribing and cautious titration are required.

questions.question: A patient recently titrated an incretin-based medicine and now has severe persistent epigastric pain, repeated vomiting, and cannot keep fluids down. What is the best FNP action?
choices: Reassure the patient and advise the next dose as scheduled
Recognize a potentially serious adverse event or acute abdominal condition and arrange urgent evaluation
Tell the patient to double the dose after symptoms resolve
Manage only with an over-the-counter antacid
questions.explanation: Severe pain, persistent vomiting, and inability to hydrate require assessment for dehydration, acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, biliary disease, obstruction, or other urgent causes.

questions.question: Why must opioid exposure be reviewed before considering naltrexone/bupropion?
choices: Naltrexone can precipitate opioid withdrawal and block opioid effects
It improves opioid analgesia
It has no interaction with opioid therapy
Only illicit opioid use matters
questions.explanation: Naltrexone can precipitate withdrawal in a patient using opioids and can interfere with opioid analgesia. Prescribing requires a complete medication and substance-use history.

questions.question: Which patient feature is a major reason to avoid or seek specialist guidance before using relevant GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 products?
choices: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2
A desire to improve mobility
Stable use of a home blood-pressure cuff
A preference for weekly rather than daily medication
questions.explanation: Relevant incretin products carry product-specific contraindications including personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2. Verify the exact label.

questions.question: Which counseling statement about weight-management medications and pregnancy is safest?
choices: They are routinely continued during pregnancy
Pregnancy intention should be assessed before treatment, and product-specific labeling and obstetric coordination guide management
Pregnancy testing is never relevant
Medication can be shared with a partner who is pregnant
questions.explanation: Weight-management medicines are not used during pregnancy. Discuss pregnancy intention and use current labeling and obstetric coordination if pregnancy is possible, planned, or confirmed.

questions.question: A patient asks to buy a compounded injectable medication from an unverified online seller because their usual product is unavailable. What is the best response?
choices: Assume it is equivalent to any FDA-approved product
Review source, exact ingredients/concentration, prescribing and pharmacy involvement, and safer alternatives; discourage unverified products
Recommend rapid dose escalation to save money
Tell the patient to share the product with family
questions.explanation: Unverified products can create concentration, ingredient, counterfeit, and safety risks. Help the patient find a safe, coordinated plan rather than improvising.

questions.question: Which issue is most important when considering phentermine-containing treatment?
choices: Cardiovascular history, blood pressure/heart rate, anxiety/insomnia, interacting medicines, and pregnancy-related requirements when applicable
Only the patient’s preferred pill color
Whether the patient dislikes injections
Whether the patient has normal bilirubin alone
questions.explanation: Sympathomimetic effects and product-specific risks make cardiovascular, psychiatric, interaction, and reproductive screening essential.

questions.question: Which situation most strongly supports referral or coordinated specialty care rather than a routine medication refill?
choices: Severe obesity-related complications, complex contraindications, suspected eating disorder, treatment nonresponse, or patient interest in bariatric evaluation
A patient asking for a copy of their weight trend
A stable patient requesting routine follow-up
A patient who prefers person-first language
questions.explanation: Referral is not failure. Complex disease, safety concerns, and patient preference often benefit from coordinated obesity, endocrine, nutrition, behavioral-health, sleep, or bariatric care.
